questions.title: Field change not seen in open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: All the following field changes are associated with open-angle glaucoma, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous field change). A nasal step is a classic early defect of open-angle glaucoma.
explanations.B: Correct. A central scotoma is the exception: glaucoma damages the arcuate nerve-fibre bundles first and spares the central (macular) fibres until late, so central vision and acuity are preserved and a central scotoma is not a typical glaucomatous defect. A central scotoma instead suggests a maculopathy or optic-nerve disease. This makes it the field change not associated with glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous field change). Arcuate (Bjerrum) scotomas follow the arcuate nerve-fibre bundles and are characteristic of glaucoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous field change). A constricted tubular field is the end-stage field of advanced glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that central vision is spared until late in glaucoma, so a central scotoma is not a glaucomatous field defect.

questions.title: Setting of phacolytic glaucoma
questions.question: Phacolytic glaucoma occurs in the setting of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. An intumescent (swollen) cataract causes phacomorphic glaucoma by angle closure, not phacolytic glaucoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Phacolytic glaucoma follows leakage through an intact but hypermature capsule; a frankly open (ruptured) capsule with lens material in the anterior chamber gives lens-particle or phaco-antigenic glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A long-standing retinal detachment is not the setting of phacolytic glaucoma.
explanations.D: Correct. Phacolytic glaucoma is a secondary open-angle glaucoma of a hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract, in which liquefied lens proteins leak through the intact capsule and, with macrophages, clog the trabecular meshwork. The raised pressure resolves after the cataract is removed. So the setting is a hypermature cataract.

questions.learning_objective: Associate phacolytic glaucoma with a hypermature cataract.

questions.title: Mechanism of glaucoma after ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion
questions.question: Which mechanism describes secondary glaucoma following ischemic central retinal vein occlusion?

options.B: Rise of IOP following a rise in systemic blood pressure
options.C: Neo-vessel formation in the anterior chamber angle

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood clogging the trabecular meshwork causes haemolytic or ghost-cell glaucoma after vitreous haemorrhage, not the glaucoma of ischaemic vein occlusion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intraocular pressure is not driven by systemic blood pressure in this way; the glaucoma here is structural, from new vessels.
explanations.C: Correct. An ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion releases angiogenic factors that grow new vessels (rubeosis) over the iris and into the anterior-chamber angle, forming a fibrovascular membrane that blocks and later contracts over the trabecular meshwork. This is neovascular glaucoma. The mechanism is neovessel formation in the angle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Angle recession is a post-traumatic tearing of the ciliary body, not the mechanism after an ischaemic vein occlusion.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute post-ischaemic-CRVO glaucoma to angle neovascularisation.

questions.title: Feature not seen in open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: Open angle glaucoma can present with all of the following, EXCEPT:

options.B: Shallow anterior chamber with iris bombe.

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a feature). A raised intraocular pressure is typical of open-angle glaucoma.
explanations.B: Correct. A shallow anterior chamber with iris bombe is the exception: open-angle glaucoma has a normal, open, deep angle, whereas a shallow chamber and iris bombe are the hallmarks of angle-closure glaucoma. So this feature does not belong to open-angle glaucoma. It is what separates the closed-angle from the open-angle mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a feature). Progressive optic-nerve damage produces glaucomatous optic atrophy with cupping.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a feature). Characteristic visual-field loss is a defining feature of open-angle glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a shallow chamber with iris bombe belongs to angle-closure, not open-angle, glaucoma.

questions.title: True statement about angle-closure glaucoma
questions.question: In angle closure glaucoma:

options.B: If medical treatment controls the high intraocular pressure, surgery is not needed.
options.C: Can be secondary to immature cataract.
options.D: Is more common in myopic women over 40 years old.

explanations.A: Correct. The definitive treatment of angle-closure glaucoma is surgical: a laser or surgical peripheral iridotomy to relieve pupil block and reopen the angle. Medical treatment only lowers the pressure acutely and does not cure the anatomical block, so the management is essentially surgical. This is the true statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Even when drops control the pressure, an iridotomy is still needed to remove the underlying pupil block, so medical control does not make surgery unnecessary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Angle closure is precipitated by an intumescent (swollen) cataract, not an immature one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Angle-closure glaucoma is commoner in hypermetropic (not myopic) older women, because hypermetropic eyes have shallow anterior chambers.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that angle-closure glaucoma is treated definitively by iridotomy, not medicine alone.

questions.title: True statement about congenital glaucoma
questions.question: Congenital glaucoma:

options.A: Should be treated by topical antiglaucoma eye drops only.
options.B: Surgical treatment is the definitive treatment.
options.C: Is best treated by lens extraction.
options.D: Does not cause blindness if not treated.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Topical drops are only a temporising measure; they do not correct the developmental angle anomaly.
explanations.B: Correct. Congenital glaucoma is caused by a developmental anomaly of the anterior-chamber angle that blocks aqueous outflow, and its definitive treatment is surgical, by goniotomy or trabeculotomy to open the obstructed angle. Drops only temporise before surgery. Early surgery is essential to prevent irreversible blindness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The problem is the angle, not the lens, so lens extraction is not the treatment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Untreated congenital glaucoma causes buphthalmos and progresses to irreversible blindness.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise surgery (goniotomy/trabeculotomy) as the definitive treatment of congenital glaucoma.

questions.title: Purpose of fundus examination in open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: Fundus examination is important in open angle glaucoma examination:

options.C: To detect any associated retinal tear.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Arteriovenous crossing changes belong to hypertensive retinopathy, not to the glaucoma assessment.
explanations.B: Correct. Fundus examination in glaucoma is done to detect optic-disc cupping, the sign of glaucomatous optic neuropathy, with an increased cup-to-disc ratio and neuroretinal-rim thinning. Following the cupping tracks the disease and its field loss. This is the reason fundoscopy is essential in glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Looking for a retinal tear is part of a peripheral retinal examination, not the purpose of fundoscopy in glaucoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The red reflex assesses the clarity of the media (for example a cataract), not the optic-disc damage of glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: State that fundoscopy in glaucoma is to detect optic-disc cupping.

questions.title: Cause not producing secondary open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: Causes of secondary open angle glaucoma include all of the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a secondary open-angle cause). Acute iridocyclitis raises the pressure with an open angle by clogging the meshwork with inflammatory cells and debris.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a secondary open-angle cause). Post-traumatic angle recession damages the trabecular meshwork, causing an open-angle glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a secondary open-angle cause). Prolonged topical steroids reduce trabecular outflow, causing steroid-induced open-angle glaucoma.
explanations.D: Correct. Phacomorphic glaucoma is the exception: it is a secondary angle-CLOSURE glaucoma, in which an intumescent (swollen) cataract pushes the iris forward and closes the angle, not an open-angle mechanism. All the other options act with an open angle, so phacomorphic glaucoma is the one that does not belong.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude phacomorphic (angle-closure) glaucoma from the causes of secondary open-angle glaucoma.

questions.title: Field change not seen in primary open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: Field changes in POAG include all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous field change). A paracentral scotoma is an early glaucomatous defect.
explanations.B: Correct. A bitemporal hemianopia is the exception: it is a chiasmal field defect from a lesion compressing the optic chiasm (classically a pituitary tumour), not a glaucomatous change. Glaucoma damages the arcuate nerve-fibre bundles and gives nasal steps, paracentral, arcuate and finally ring or tubular defects that respect the horizontal meridian. So a bitemporal hemianopia does not belong to glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous field change). Arcuate (Bjerrum) scotomas follow the arcuate nerve-fibre bundles and are characteristic of glaucoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous field change). A ring scotoma forms when superior and inferior arcuate scotomas join in advanced glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish glaucomatous field loss (nasal step, arcuate and ring scotoma) from a chiasmal bitemporal hemianopia.

questions.title: Test not used to diagnose glaucoma
questions.question: To diagnose glaucoma the following are used, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is used). Applanation tonometry measures the intraocular pressure.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is used). Perimetry maps the characteristic glaucomatous field loss.
explanations.C: Correct. Fluorescein angiography is the exception: it images the retinal and choroidal circulation for vascular and macular disease and has no role in diagnosing glaucoma. Glaucoma is diagnosed by tonometry, perimetry, gonioscopy and optic-disc (fundus) examination. So fluorescein angiography is the tool not used.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is used). Fundus examination assesses the optic-disc cupping of glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude fluorescein angiography from the tools used to diagnose glaucoma.

questions.title: True statement about primary open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: One of the following is TRUE about primary open-angle glaucoma:

options.C: It requires surgery in most cases.
options.D: Gonioscopy reveals a prominent Schwalbe's line.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Primary open-angle glaucoma is painless and does not typically present with headache.
explanations.B: Correct. Optic-disc analysis is mandatory in primary open-angle glaucoma because the disease is asymptomatic until late and cannot be found from symptoms. Assessing the cup-to-disc ratio and neuroretinal rim, with tonometry and perimetry, is how the disease is detected and followed. So disc analysis being mandatory is the true statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Most cases are controlled medically; surgery is reserved for progression or intolerance, not the majority.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A prominent Schwalbe line (posterior embryotoxon) is an angle anomaly, not a feature of the open, normal angle of POAG.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that POAG is asymptomatic early, making optic-disc analysis mandatory.

questions.title: Lens-induced glaucoma of a hypermature cataract
questions.question: Lens induced glaucoma that occurs with hypermature cataract is called:

explanations.A: Correct. Phacolytic glaucoma is the lens-induced glaucoma of a hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract: liquefied lens proteins leak through the intact capsule and, with macrophages, block the trabecular meshwork. It is a secondary open-angle glaucoma that resolves once the cataract is removed. So the hypermature-cataract glaucoma is phacolytic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neovascular glaucoma follows angle neovascularisation after retinal ischaemia, not a hypermature lens.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phacomorphic glaucoma follows an intumescent (swollen) cataract closing the angle, not a hypermature one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Uveitic glaucoma follows intraocular inflammation, not a hypermature lens.

questions.learning_objective: Name phacolytic glaucoma as the lens-induced glaucoma of a hypermature cataract.

questions.title: Condition not causing secondary glaucoma
questions.question: Secondary glaucoma may develop after all of the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it can cause it). Uveitis clogs the meshwork with inflammatory cells and forms synechiae, causing secondary glaucoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it can cause it). Prolonged steroids reduce trabecular outflow, causing steroid-induced glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it can cause it). Proliferative diabetic retinopathy causes neovascular glaucoma through angle neovascularisation.
explanations.D: Correct. Entropion is the exception: it is an inward rolling of the eyelid margin, a lid disorder that irritates the cornea but has nothing to do with the intraocular pressure or the drainage angle. All the other options obstruct aqueous outflow and raise the pressure, whereas entropion does not. So entropion does not cause secondary glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude entropion (a lid disorder) from the causes of secondary glaucoma.

questions.title: Sign not seen in glaucomatous optic neuropathy
questions.question: The clinical picture of glaucomatous optic neuropathy includes the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a sign). A bared, overhanging (bayoneting) disc edge is a glaucomatous sign.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a sign). A large deep cup with rim thinning is the hallmark of glaucomatous cupping.
explanations.C: Correct. Sheathing of the retinal vessels is the exception: perivascular sheathing is a sign of vascular or inflammatory retinopathy, not of glaucomatous optic neuropathy. The glaucomatous disc instead shows a large deep cup, an overhanging edge, rim thinning and a visible lamina cribrosa. So vessel sheathing is not a glaucoma sign.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a sign). A visible (well-seen) lamina cribrosa, the laminar-dot sign, is exposed by glaucomatous cupping.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the glaucomatous disc signs and exclude retinal-vessel sheathing.

questions.title: Not a medical treatment of open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: Medical treatment of open angle glaucoma includes the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a treatment). Prostaglandin analogues lower pressure by increasing uveoscleral outflow.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a treatment). Beta-blockers lower pressure by reducing aqueous formation.
explanations.C: Correct. Topical steroids are the exception: far from treating open-angle glaucoma, they raise the intraocular pressure in steroid responders and cause steroid-induced glaucoma. The antiglaucoma classes are prostaglandin analogues, beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and alpha-agonists. So topical steroids are not a treatment.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a treatment). Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors lower pressure by reducing aqueous formation.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude topical steroids from the medical treatment of open-angle glaucoma.

questions.title: Cause of blindness among the options
questions.question: Blindness can result from:

options.B: Using diseased eyes for a long time.
options.C: Holding books too close to the eye while reading for a long time.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Using a mobile phone does not cause blindness.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 'Using diseased eyes' is not a mechanism of blindness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Holding books close causes eye strain, not blindness.
explanations.D: Correct. Untreated progressive glaucoma leads to irreversible blindness: sustained raised pressure destroys the optic-nerve fibres and the resulting field loss cannot be recovered. It is a leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide, which is why early detection and pressure control matter. So the cause of blindness here is untreated progressive glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise untreated progressive glaucoma as a cause of irreversible blindness.

questions.title: Drainage route of aqueous humour
questions.question: Aqueous humor is drained through:

explanations.A: Correct. Aqueous humour is drained at the angle of the anterior chamber, through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm canal and on to the episcleral veins. It is secreted by the ciliary body into the posterior chamber and flows through the pupil before draining at this angle. So the drainage site is the anterior-chamber angle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ciliary body secretes aqueous; it does not drain it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior surface of the iris is not a drainage route.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lens plays no part in aqueous drainage.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the anterior-chamber angle as the drainage route of aqueous humour.

questions.title: Investigation not used in glaucoma diagnosis
questions.question: All of the following are important for diagnosis of glaucoma, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is used). Applanation tonometry measures the intraocular pressure.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is used). Perimetry maps the glaucomatous field loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is used). Gonioscopy shows whether the drainage angle is open or closed.
explanations.D: Correct. Fluorescein angiography is the exception: it is a retinal vascular investigation with no role in diagnosing glaucoma. The glaucoma work-up is tonometry, perimetry, gonioscopy and optic-disc examination. So fluorescein angiography is the one not used.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude fluorescein angiography from the glaucoma diagnostic work-up.

questions.title: Lens-induced glaucoma of an intumescent cataract
questions.question: Lens induced glaucoma that occurs with intumescent cataract is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phacolytic glaucoma follows a hypermature cataract, not an intumescent one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neovascular glaucoma follows retinal ischaemia, not a swollen lens.
explanations.C: Correct. Phacomorphic glaucoma is the lens-induced glaucoma of an intumescent (swollen) cataract: the enlarged lens pushes the iris forward and closes the angle, a secondary angle-closure glaucoma. It is relieved by removing the cataract after controlling the pressure. So the intumescent-cataract glaucoma is phacomorphic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Uveitic glaucoma follows intraocular inflammation, not an intumescent lens.

questions.learning_objective: Name phacomorphic glaucoma as the lens-induced glaucoma of an intumescent cataract.

questions.title: Defective vision in a child on long-term steroids for spring catarrh
questions.question: A 12-year-old boy receiving long term steroid treatment for spring catarrh and used to excessively rub his eyes developed defective vision in both eyes. The likely cause is:

explanations.A: Correct. A child on long-term topical steroids for vernal (spring) catarrh is at risk of steroid-induced secondary glaucoma, a steroid response that reduces trabecular outflow and raises the pressure in both treated eyes. The bilateral defective vision after prolonged steroid use points to this rather than to a unilateral or vascular cause. So the likely cause is secondary glaucoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Retinopathy of prematurity affects premature neonates, not a 12-year-old.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Optic neuritis is usually unilateral with pain on eye movement, not a bilateral steroid complication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitreous haemorrhage is not a recognised consequence of topical steroid use for spring catarrh.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute bilateral visual loss after prolonged steroids for spring catarrh to secondary (steroid-induced) glaucoma.

questions.title: False statement about aqueous humour
questions.question: Regarding aqueous humor, all is true, EXCEPT:

options.A: Is produced by the ciliary body of the eye.
options.B: Is drained through the trabecular meshwork in the angle of the posterior chamber.
options.C: Drains mostly to the episcleral veins.
options.D: IOP is maintained by balance between its formation and drainage.

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is true). Aqueous is produced by the ciliary body.
explanations.B: Correct. The statement is false because the trabecular meshwork lies in the angle of the ANTERIOR chamber, not the posterior chamber. Aqueous is secreted into the posterior chamber but drains at the anterior-chamber angle through the meshwork into Schlemm canal. So placing the meshwork in the posterior-chamber angle is the untrue statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is true). Aqueous drains through Schlemm canal mostly to the episcleral veins.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is true). Intraocular pressure is maintained by the balance between aqueous formation and drainage.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the trabecular meshwork drains aqueous at the anterior- (not posterior-) chamber angle.

questions.title: Not a risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: All of the following are considered risk factors for POAG, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a risk factor). Increasing age raises the risk of POAG.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a risk factor). A positive family history raises the risk of POAG.
explanations.C: Correct. Male gender is the exception: sex is not an established risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma. The recognised risk factors are increasing age, a positive family history, raised intraocular pressure, myopia and African ancestry. So male gender is not a risk factor.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a risk factor). Myopia is a recognised risk factor for POAG.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude male gender from the risk factors for POAG (age, family history, myopia).

questions.title: Treatment of phacolytic glaucoma
questions.question: Phakolytic glaucoma is best treated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A fistulising drainage operation does not remove the leaking lens proteins that cause phacolytic glaucoma.
explanations.B: Correct. Phacolytic glaucoma is caused by leaked proteins of a hypermature cataract blocking the meshwork, so its definitive treatment is cataract extraction to remove the source, after the pressure is first controlled medically. Removing the cataract cures the glaucoma. So the treatment is cataract extraction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A cyclodestructive procedure is reserved for refractory or blind painful eyes, not first-line phacolytic glaucoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Miotics and beta-blockers only temporise; they do not remove the offending lens.

questions.learning_objective: State that phacolytic (lens-induced) glaucoma is treated by cataract extraction.

questions.title: Antecedent of neovascular glaucoma
questions.question: Neovascular glaucoma follows:

explanations.A: Correct. Neovascular glaucoma follows an ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion (thrombosis): the ischaemic retina releases angiogenic factors that grow new vessels over the iris and angle, blocking outflow. It is the classic cause of rubeotic glaucoma. So it follows central retinal vein thrombosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute congestive (angle-closure) glaucoma is a primary angle-closure, not the cause of neovascular glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Staphylococcal infection causes lid and orbital infection, not neovascular glaucoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Systemic hypertension alone does not cause neovascular glaucoma; retinal ischaemia does.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute neovascular glaucoma to ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion.

questions.title: Not a treatment option in POAG
questions.question: Treatment options in POAG may include all, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a treatment). Beta-blockers reduce aqueous formation.
explanations.B: Correct. 'Anti-prostaglandin' is the exception: the antiglaucoma drug is a prostaglandin analogue (an agonist) that increases uveoscleral outflow, not a prostaglandin antagonist. The other listed classes, beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and alpha-agonists, are all genuine antiglaucoma drugs. So 'anti-prostaglandin' is not a treatment option.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a treatment). Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce aqueous formation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a treatment). Alpha-adrenergic agonists reduce formation and increase outflow.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the antiglaucoma drug is a prostaglandin analogue, not an 'anti-prostaglandin'.

questions.hold: Printed key marks anterior lens dislocation (b) as the LEAST likely cause of lens-induced glaucoma, which contradicts the option text: anterior lens dislocation classically causes pupillary-block angle-closure glaucoma, whereas posterior subcapsular cataract (c) does not cause lens-induced glaucoma at all. Key-vs-option contradiction; held per the never-guess rule. Key for reference Q26.B.

questions.title: Important point in diagnosing open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: Which of the following would be an important point in diagnosing a case of open angle glaucoma?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A shallow anterior chamber is a feature of angle-closure, not open-angle, glaucoma.
explanations.B: Correct. Optic-disc cupping is the key diagnostic sign of open-angle glaucoma, reflecting the glaucomatous optic neuropathy that defines the disease. Because the angle is open and the eye is white and quiet, the diagnosis rests on the disc and the field rather than on angle signs. So disc cupping is the important diagnostic point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A narrow angle points to angle-closure glaucoma, not open-angle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Visual acuity and refractive error are preserved until late and do not diagnose open-angle glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Identify optic-disc cupping as the key diagnostic sign of open-angle glaucoma.

questions.title: Lens problem most likely to cause secondary angle-closure
questions.question: The following type of lens problem is the most likely to result in secondary angle closure glaucoma:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A hypermature cataract causes phacolytic (open-angle) glaucoma, not angle closure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A traumatic cataract more often causes angle recession or lens-particle open-angle glaucoma.
explanations.C: Correct. An intumescent (swollen) cataract is the lens problem most likely to cause secondary angle-closure glaucoma: the enlarged lens pushes the iris forward and closes the drainage angle, i.e. phacomorphic glaucoma. Removing the cataract relieves the closure. So the intumescent cataract is the answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. After-cataract (posterior capsular opacification) blurs vision but does not close the angle.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the intumescent cataract as the lens problem causing secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.title: True statement about primary open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: The following is true about primary open angle glaucoma:

options.B: It is asymptomatic in its early stages.
options.C: It requires surgery in most cases.
options.D: Gonioscopy reveals a prominent Schwalbe's line.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Primary open-angle glaucoma is painless and does not usually present with headache.
explanations.B: Correct. Primary open-angle glaucoma is asymptomatic in its early stages: the eye is white and quiet and central acuity is preserved, so the patient notices nothing until the field is badly damaged. This silence is why screening by pressure, disc and field examination is essential. So being asymptomatic early is the true statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Most cases are controlled medically; surgery is not required in the majority.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A prominent Schwalbe line is an angle anomaly, not a feature of the open, normal angle of POAG.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that POAG is asymptomatic in its early stages.

questions.title: Eye drops that may cause glaucoma
questions.question: Which of the following eye drops may result in glaucoma:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Antiviral drops do not raise intraocular pressure.
explanations.B: Correct. Topical steroid drops can result in glaucoma: in steroid responders they reduce trabecular outflow and raise the intraocular pressure, causing steroid-induced open-angle glaucoma. The risk grows with prolonged use. So steroids are the drops that may cause glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Topical NSAIDs do not cause a steroid-response rise in pressure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sulphonamide drops do not raise intraocular pressure by a steroid mechanism.

questions.learning_objective: Identify topical steroids as the eye drops that may cause glaucoma.

questions.hold: The EXCEPT/true-statement stem about neovascular glaucoma has two defensibly false options: the keyed 'It often results from central retinal artery occlusion' (a) is false (NVG follows ischaemic central retinal VEIN occlusion), but 'Miotics are useful for treatment' (d) is also false (miotics are not useful in neovascular glaucoma). Not single-best as printed; held for adjudication. Key for reference Q31.A.

questions.title: Surgery using mitomycin C as an adjunct
questions.question: Mitomycin C is used as an adjunct to which of the following surgeries:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitrectomy is a posterior-segment operation that does not use mitomycin C as a routine adjunct.
explanations.B: Correct. Mitomycin C is used as an intraoperative adjunct to trabeculectomy, the filtering glaucoma operation, to inhibit fibroblast proliferation and prevent scarring of the drainage bleb. Reducing scarring improves the long-term success of the filter. So mitomycin C is the adjunct to trabeculectomy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Goniotomy for congenital glaucoma does not use mitomycin C.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Keratoplasty (corneal grafting) is not the mitomycin-C glaucoma operation.

questions.learning_objective: Associate mitomycin C with trabeculectomy as an antiscarring adjunct.

questions.title: Complication not caused by a hypermature cataract
questions.question: Hypermature cataract can cause the following complications, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. Phacomorphic glaucoma is the exception: it is caused by an intumescent (swollen) cataract closing the angle, not by a hypermature cataract. A hypermature cataract instead causes phacolytic glaucoma, phacotoxic (lens-protein) iridocyclitis and, as its zonules weaken, lens dislocation. So phacomorphic glaucoma is the complication that does not belong to a hypermature cataract.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a complication). Leaked lens proteins of a hypermature cataract cause phacotoxic iridocyclitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a complication). A hypermature cataract can dislocate as its zonules degenerate.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a complication). A hypermature cataract causes phacolytic glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude phacomorphic glaucoma (an intumescent-cataract disease) from the complications of a hypermature cataract.

questions.title: Vision in absolute glaucoma
questions.question: In absolute glaucoma the vision:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Counting fingers implies residual vision, which absolute glaucoma has lost.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hand movements implies residual vision, which absolute glaucoma has lost.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Just perception of light still implies some retained function; absolute glaucoma has none.
explanations.D: Correct. In absolute glaucoma the vision is no perception of light: it is the end stage of uncontrolled glaucoma in which the optic nerve is wholly destroyed and the eye is blind. It is often a painful blind eye treated only for comfort. So the vision is no perception of light.

questions.learning_objective: Define absolute glaucoma as the end-stage eye with no perception of light.

questions.title: Glaucoma caused by an intumescent cataract
questions.question: Which type of glaucoma is caused by intumescent cataract?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phacolytic glaucoma follows a hypermature cataract, not an intumescent one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Phacoanaphylactic (lens-induced uveitis) glaucoma follows a ruptured capsule with an autoimmune reaction, not an intumescent lens.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma is caused by fibrillar material on the lens and angle, not by lens swelling.
explanations.D: Correct. Phacomorphic glaucoma is caused by an intumescent (swollen) cataract: the enlarged lens pushes the iris forward and closes the angle, a secondary angle-closure glaucoma. It is relieved by cataract extraction. So the intumescent-cataract glaucoma is phacomorphic.

questions.learning_objective: Name phacomorphic glaucoma as the glaucoma caused by an intumescent cataract.

questions.hold: Answer-key table omits the Q36 row (it skips from Q35 to Q37); no printed key to re-verify against, held per the never-guess rule. (Stem: glaucoma caused by anterior lens dislocation.)

questions.title: Procedure that is not a glaucoma operation
questions.question: Glaucoma surgeries include all of the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a glaucoma operation). Trabeculectomy is the standard filtering procedure for adult glaucoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a glaucoma operation). Goniotomy opens the malformed angle in congenital glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a glaucoma operation). A peripheral iridectomy relieves pupil block in angle-closure glaucoma.
explanations.D: Correct. Blepharoplasty is the exception: it is eyelid surgery that removes redundant lid skin and does nothing to intraocular pressure. Glaucoma operations instead work by improving aqueous drainage or relieving pupil block, as with trabeculectomy, goniotomy and iridectomy. So blepharoplasty is not a glaucoma procedure.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise blepharoplasty as an eyelid, not a glaucoma, operation.

questions.title: Wrong statement about the visual field in glaucoma
questions.question: Which of the following statements is WRONG?

options.A: Only the central field is important in glaucoma
options.B: Peripheral field changes occur in glaucoma
options.C: Enlargement of the blind spot is a glaucomatous field change
options.D: Tubular fields can occur in glaucoma

explanations.A: Correct. This is the wrong statement: glaucoma damages the peripheral (arcuate) nerve-fibre bundles first, so the peripheral field is the important one to monitor, and central vision is preserved until end-stage. Saying only the central field matters inverts the natural history of the disease. It would cause early field loss to be missed.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true statement). Peripheral field defects such as the nasal step are the earliest glaucomatous changes.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true statement). Enlargement of the blind spot is a recognised early glaucomatous field change.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true statement). A constricted tubular field is the end-stage glaucomatous field.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that glaucoma affects the peripheral field first, sparing central vision until late.

questions.title: Antiglaucoma drug that does not reduce aqueous formation
questions.question: Which of the following drugs does NOT decrease aqueous formation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Topical beta blockers lower pressure by reducing aqueous secretion by the ciliary epithelium.
explanations.B: Correct. Prostaglandin analogues are the exception: they lower intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous, not by reducing its formation. The other three classes all suppress aqueous secretion. So the prostaglandin analogue is the drug that does not decrease aqueous production.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce aqueous formation by blocking bicarbonate production in the ciliary body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alpha-adrenergic agonists such as brimonidine both reduce aqueous formation and increase uveoscleral outflow.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish prostaglandin analogues (increase outflow) from the aqueous-suppressant antiglaucoma classes.

questions.title: Drug that can raise the intraocular pressure
questions.question: Which of the following drugs can lead to a rise of intraocular pressure?

explanations.A: Correct. Steroids can raise intraocular pressure: in susceptible (steroid-responder) patients they reduce outflow through the trabecular meshwork and cause a secondary open-angle (steroid-induced) glaucoma. The other three drugs all lower pressure. So steroids are the pressure-raising drug.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beta blockers lower pressure by reducing aqueous formation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Brimonidine, an alpha-2 agonist, lowers pressure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mannitol is an osmotic agent used to lower a dangerously high pressure acutely.

questions.learning_objective: Identify steroids as the drug that raises, rather than lowers, intraocular pressure.

questions.hold: Bank item is a two-option True/False statement (a True, b False) about vision in absolute glaucoma; below the four-option MCQ floor the emitter enforces, so it cannot be authored as a single-best-answer item. Key for reference Q41.B.

questions.title: Not a cause of secondary glaucoma
questions.question: Causes of secondary glaucoma do NOT include:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a cause). A severe corneal ulcer with inflammation can raise pressure and cause secondary glaucoma.
explanations.B: Correct. A mature senile cataract is the exception: it is fully opaque but neither swollen nor hypermature, so it does not obstruct aqueous outflow. Lens-induced glaucoma needs an intumescent (swollen) cataract for phacomorphic angle closure or a hypermature (leaking) cataract for phacolytic glaucoma. A plain mature cataract therefore does not cause secondary glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a cause). Iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis) causes secondary glaucoma through inflammatory debris and synechiae.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a cause). Ischaemic central retinal vein thrombosis leads to neovascular glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a mature (not intumescent or hypermature) cataract does not cause secondary glaucoma.

questions.title: Occlusion least likely to cause neovascular glaucoma
questions.question: Neovascular glaucoma is least likely to occur as a result of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion is a classic cause of neovascular glaucoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A central retinal artery occlusion produces widespread retinal ischaemia and can drive angle neovascularisation.
explanations.C: Correct. A branch retinal artery occlusion is least likely: it infarcts only a sector of retina, so the area of ischaemia and the angiogenic drive are small and rarely enough to produce rubeosis and neovascular glaucoma. The large-territory ischaemia of a central vein occlusion, central artery occlusion or diabetic retinopathy is far more likely to. So the branch occlusion is the least likely cause.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of neovascular glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Rank the ischaemic causes of neovascular glaucoma and identify branch arterial occlusion as least likely.

questions.title: Not a cause of secondary open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: The most important causes of secondary OPEN-angle glaucoma include all of the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a secondary open-angle cause). Phacolytic glaucoma clogs the open trabecular meshwork with leaked lens proteins.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a secondary open-angle cause). Steroids reduce trabecular outflow through an open angle.
explanations.C: Correct. Phacomorphic glaucoma is the exception: an intumescent cataract pushes the iris forward and closes the angle, so it is a secondary ANGLE-CLOSURE, not open-angle, glaucoma. The others all raise pressure through an open angle. So phacomorphic glaucoma does not belong on the open-angle list.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a secondary open-angle cause). Angle recession damages the trabecular meshwork of an anatomically open angle.

questions.learning_objective: Separate phacomorphic (angle-closure) from the secondary open-angle mechanisms.

questions.title: Investigation used to diagnose glaucoma
questions.question: An investigation needed for the diagnosis of glaucoma includes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. OCT of the macula assesses macular disease; glaucoma is followed with OCT of the optic nerve/RNFL, not the macula.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fundus fluorescein angiography images retinal vasculature and is not a glaucoma test.
explanations.C: Correct. Visual field testing (perimetry) is a core investigation for diagnosing and staging glaucoma, because it maps the characteristic arcuate and nasal-step defects of glaucomatous nerve-fibre loss. Together with tonometry and optic-disc assessment it confirms the diagnosis. So the visual field is the needed investigation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ocular ultrasound (B-scan) images the posterior segment when the media are opaque and is not used to diagnose glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Select visual-field testing as a core glaucoma investigation.

questions.title: Normal range of intraocular pressure
questions.question: The following is the normal range of intraocular pressure:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 120/80 mmHg is a systemic arterial blood-pressure figure, meaningless for the eye.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 90/60 mmHg is again a systemic blood-pressure reading, not an intraocular pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4-28 mmHg is too wide; the upper figure is well into the pathological range.
explanations.D: Correct. The normal intraocular pressure is about 8-21 mmHg, measured as a single value (not a ratio), with only a small diurnal variation and little difference between the eyes. Readings above this band raise suspicion of glaucoma, though a pressure is ultimately judged normal by whether it damages the optic nerve. So 8-21 mmHg is the normal range.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal intraocular pressure as roughly 8-21 mmHg.

questions.hold: Statement-set item on treatment of OAG: the four lettered options are separate assertions of which more than one is defensibly true (lack-of-compliance surgery AND long-term systemic CAI caveats), not single-best as printed. Held for adjudication. Key for reference Q57.A.

questions.title: Steroids and secondary open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: As regards secondary glaucoma, which statement is true?

options.A: Secondary angle-closure glaucoma may occur with prolonged use of topical steroids
options.B: Secondary open-angle glaucoma may occur with prolonged use of topical steroids
options.D: Patients do not develop glaucoma a long time after blunt trauma

explanations.A: Incorrect. Steroids raise pressure through an open angle by reducing trabecular outflow, so the mechanism is open-angle, not angle-closure.
explanations.B: Correct. Prolonged topical steroids cause a secondary OPEN-angle glaucoma in steroid-responders: the drug reduces aqueous outflow through an anatomically open trabecular meshwork, raising the pressure. Stopping the steroid usually returns the pressure toward normal. So this is the true statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Topical steroids are a well-recognised cause of glaucoma, so 'never' is false.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Angle-recession glaucoma can appear years after blunt trauma, so late post-traumatic glaucoma does occur.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise prolonged topical steroids as a cause of secondary open-angle glaucoma.

questions.title: Glaucoma that is not a painful red eye
questions.question: Painful red eyes do NOT occur with:

explanations.A: Correct. Primary open-angle glaucoma is the exception: the pressure rises slowly, so the eye stays white and painless and the vision is lost insidiously. The other three raise pressure abruptly or inflame the eye and present as a painful red eye. So a painful red eye is not a feature of open-angle glaucoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute primary angle-closure is the classic painful red eye with a high pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secondary angle-closure glaucoma likewise presents with a painful red eye.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neovascular glaucoma is a painful red eye from rubeosis and very high pressure.

questions.learning_objective: Contrast the painless white eye of open-angle glaucoma with the painful red angle-closure and neovascular glaucomas.

questions.title: Risk factor for open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: As regards open-angle glaucoma (OAG):

options.A: It is symptomatic in early stages

explanations.A: Incorrect. Open-angle glaucoma is asymptomatic in early stages, which is why it is caught on screening.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Treatment is mainly medical (pressure-lowering drops) first, with surgery reserved for failure of medical control.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Astigmatism is a refractive error unrelated to open-angle glaucoma risk.
explanations.D: Correct. Myopia is a recognised risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma, alongside older age, a positive family history, raised intraocular pressure, diabetes and African ancestry. Myopic eyes have discs more susceptible to pressure-related damage. So myopia is the true risk factor here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify myopia as a risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma.

questions.hold: Statement-set item ('treatment of POAG is mainly medical in the following conditions'): the keyed option (progressive nerve-fibre damage on minimum tolerated medical treatment) actually indicates SURGERY, not continued medical treatment, so the key contradicts the stem; more than one option is defensibly arguable. Held for adjudication. Key for reference Q61.C.

questions.title: Condition not causing secondary glaucoma
questions.question: Secondary glaucoma may occur in all of the following conditions, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a cause). Blood cells from a hyphema block the trabecular meshwork and raise pressure.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a cause). Iritis (anterior uveitis) causes secondary glaucoma through inflammatory cells and synechiae.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a cause). An intumescent (swollen) cataract closes the angle and causes phacomorphic glaucoma.
explanations.D: Correct. An immature cataract is the exception: it is only partially opaque and neither swollen nor leaking, so it does not obstruct aqueous outflow or cause glaucoma. Lens-induced glaucoma needs an intumescent or hypermature lens. So an immature cataract does not cause secondary glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that an immature cataract does not cause secondary glaucoma.

questions.title: Cause least likely to give neovascular glaucoma
questions.question: Neovascular glaucoma is less likely to occur as a result of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is a major cause of neovascular glaucoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion is a classic cause.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Retinal ischaemia is the common final pathway that drives angle neovascularisation.
explanations.D: Correct. A mature cataract is the exception: it is a lens opacity with no retinal ischaemia, so it releases no angiogenic factors and does not cause rubeosis or neovascular glaucoma. The other three all produce the retinal ischaemia that drives new-vessel formation. So a mature cataract is the least likely cause.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that neovascular glaucoma arises from retinal ischaemia, not from a cataract.

questions.title: Cataract that causes lens-induced glaucoma
questions.question: Lens-induced glaucoma occurs in the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect. An anterior polar cataract is a small stationary opacity that does not raise pressure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A posterior subcapsular cataract impairs vision but does not cause lens-induced glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A nuclear cataract causes an index myopic shift, not glaucoma.
explanations.D: Correct. A hypermature cataract causes lens-induced (phacolytic) glaucoma: liquefied lens proteins leak through the intact capsule and, with macrophages, clog the trabecular meshwork and raise the pressure. An intumescent lens likewise causes phacomorphic angle closure. So the hypermature cataract is the lens that causes glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Associate lens-induced glaucoma with a hypermature (or intumescent) cataract.

questions.title: When intraocular pressure is considered normal
questions.question: For the intraocular pressure to be considered normal, the:

options.A: Difference between the two eyes should be more than 3 mmHg
options.B: Diurnal variation does not exceed 7 mmHg
options.D: IOP is considered normal if it is not damaging the optic nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inter-eye difference should be SMALL (a few mmHg); a difference greater than about 3-4 mmHg is suspicious, not normal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The normal diurnal variation is only a few mmHg (about 3-5); a swing this large is not the defining criterion of normality.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The quoted band is inaccurate; the accepted statistical range is about 8-21 (10-21) mmHg.
explanations.D: Correct. The functional definition is that a pressure is normal when it does not damage the optic nerve. This is why some eyes tolerate statistically high readings (ocular hypertension) while others are damaged within the normal band (normal-tension glaucoma). So normality is judged by optic-nerve safety, not a single number.

questions.learning_objective: Define a normal intraocular pressure functionally, as one that does not damage the optic nerve.

questions.hold: Statement-set item on POAG: the four lettered options are separate assertions, more than one defensibly evaluable and the keyed answer (6/6 maintained till late) sits among other partly-true statements; not single-best as printed. Held for adjudication. Key for reference Q66.B.

questions.title: Important point in diagnosing open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: An important point in diagnosing open-angle glaucoma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Open-angle glaucoma has a normal deep chamber; a shallow chamber suggests angle closure.
explanations.B: Correct. Optic-disc cupping is a key diagnostic sign of open-angle glaucoma: progressive loss of neuroretinal rim enlarges the cup, raising the cup-disc ratio and producing the characteristic glaucomatous disc. It is assessed alongside the intraocular pressure and visual field. So disc cupping is the important diagnostic point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A narrow angle is the hallmark of angle-closure, not open-angle, glaucoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Central visual acuity and refractive error are typically preserved until late and are not diagnostic of open-angle glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise optic-disc cupping as a central diagnostic feature of open-angle glaucoma.

questions.title: Field change not seen in open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: The following field changes are associated with open-angle glaucoma, EXCEPT:

options.D: Early loss of the central field

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous change). A nasal step is a classic early defect.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous change). An arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma follows the arcuate nerve-fibre bundles.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a glaucomatous change). Tubular (tunnel) vision is the end-stage constricted field.
explanations.D: Correct. Early loss of the central field is the exception: glaucoma damages the arcuate bundles first and spares the central (macular) fibres until end-stage, so central vision and acuity are preserved early. Early central loss instead suggests a maculopathy or optic-nerve disease. So it is not an early glaucomatous field change.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that central vision is preserved early in glaucoma, so early central field loss is not glaucomatous.

questions.title: Field change that is seen in open-angle glaucoma
questions.question: The following is a field change associated with open-angle glaucoma:

options.D: Early loss of the central field

explanations.A: Incorrect. The characteristic step in glaucoma is a NASAL step, not a temporal one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An altitudinal field defect points to ischaemic optic neuropathy or a retinal vascular occlusion, not glaucoma.
explanations.C: Correct. An arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma is a characteristic glaucomatous field defect: it follows the arc of the retinal nerve-fibre bundles that glaucoma damages, sweeping from the blind spot around the central field. With the nasal step it is one of the early defects of glaucoma. So the arcuate scotoma is the glaucomatous change.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Central vision is spared until late in glaucoma, so early central loss is not glaucomatous.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the arcuate scotoma as a characteristic glaucomatous field defect.

questions.title: Cataract that does not cause lens-induced glaucoma
questions.question: Lens-induced glaucoma occurs in all of the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it can cause it). A traumatic cataract can release lens material that blocks the meshwork (lens-particle glaucoma).
explanations.B: Correct. A posterior subcapsular cataract is the exception: it is a thin opacity at the back of the lens that impairs vision but does not swell or leak, so it does not obstruct aqueous outflow or cause glaucoma. Lens-induced glaucoma needs an intumescent, hypermature or ruptured lens. So the posterior subcapsular cataract does not cause it.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it can cause it). An intumescent (swollen) cataract closes the angle and causes phacomorphic glaucoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it can cause it). A hypermature cataract leaks proteins and causes phacolytic glaucoma.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a posterior subcapsular cataract does not cause lens-induced glaucoma.

questions.title: Correct statement about phacomorphic glaucoma
questions.question: As regards phacomorphic glaucoma, which of the following is correct?

options.A: It is treated by cataract extraction
options.B: It is due to a hypermature cataract
options.C: It is associated with an open angle
options.D: There is a deep anterior chamber

explanations.A: Correct. Phacomorphic glaucoma is treated by cataract extraction: removing the swollen intumescent lens relieves the pupil block and reopens the closed angle, curing the glaucoma. Pressure-lowering drops only temporise before surgery. So cataract extraction is the definitive treatment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Phacomorphic glaucoma is caused by an intumescent (swollen) cataract; a hypermature cataract causes phacolytic glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The swollen lens pushes the iris forward and CLOSES the angle, so it is an angle-closure, not open-angle, glaucoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior chamber is SHALLOW, because the intumescent lens crowds the angle forward.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that phacomorphic glaucoma is a shallow-chamber angle-closure treated by cataract extraction.
